title: District of Columbia State Government Websites: ADA Title II PDF Accessibility | SignalFeed.dev
description: How District of Columbia state-government websites stand on PDF accessibility before the April 26, 2027 ADA Title II date: 37% of 147 sampled PDFs untagged, 4% scanned. Aggregate, automated signals.
h1: District of Columbia: Title II PDF backlog on state government websites
body:
We found 6 working state-government websites on .gov domains registered to District of Columbia in CISA's public .gov registry. State governments are Title II public entities, and all of them reach the ADA Title II web rule's compliance date on April 26, 2027 (28 CFR part 35, subpart H): web content, PDFs included, must conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, subject to the rule's exceptions.

Does ADA Title II apply to District of Columbia?

Yes. Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act is federal law and covers every state and local government in every state: District of Columbia's state agencies and public universities, counties, cities, towns, school districts and special districts. The 2024 web rule adds technical requirements for their websites, apps and the documents they post (WCAG 2.1 Level AA). Its compliance date depends on population: April 26, 2027 for governments serving 50,000 or more people (every state government included), April 26, 2028 for smaller ones and for special districts. This is general information, not legal advice.

We measured the PDFs these sites link from their pages. This page summarizes District of Columbia's state-government sites as a whole. It does not name or rank individual agencies. Agencies on non-.gov addresses are not included. For cities and counties, see the city and county editions.

District of Columbia at a glance

  • 3 of 6 state-government sites measured with a usable sample (20 or more PDFs). The rest blocked automated visitors, host documents on other systems, or had too few PDFs to sample; that is not a clean result.
  • 147 PDFs analyzed. 36.7% had no accessibility tags, close to the national figure of 37.7%. 4.1% were scanned images with no usable text, and 42.2% did not declare a document language.
  • 0 of 9 sampled PDFs passed the veraPDF PDF/UA-1 checks.
  • The median measured site has roughly 668 pages of PDFs failing at least one basic check; across the measured sites that is on the order of 1,800 pages.
  • 36% of the sampled PDFs were modified in 2024 or later. Recent documents are more likely to still be in active use, and documents used to apply for, access or participate in a service are not covered by the rule's exception for preexisting documents.

What this means for District of Columbia agencies

An untagged PDF gives a screen reader no headings, no reading order and no table structure. A scanned PDF gives it nothing at all. Both typically fail WCAG 2.1 AA (for example 1.3.1 Info and Relationships, and for scans 1.1.1 Non-text Content), and both are common in reports, rules, forms and notices.

Not every old PDF has to be fixed. The rule exempts archived web content and preexisting conventional electronic documents unless they are currently used to apply for, access or participate in a service. The practical order is usually: fix the export settings so new documents are born accessible, remediate forms and anything people use to get a service, and move true archives to a clearly marked archive section. Our ADA Title II PDF guide walks through it.

For agendas, minutes and notices, our accessible meeting templates for small public bodies ($24, Word + PDF/UA) export tagged PDFs from Word, so new documents start out accessible.

What this is, and what it isn't

These are automated signals, not a conformance evaluation. An automated check can show that a PDF fails; it cannot show that a PDF conforms. Estimates are scaled from samples, and a few very long documents can move a number a lot. The full method is on the national Backlog Index page.
